title: Those cheese crystals are not salt

sources.title: Parmigiano Reggiano Consortium FAQ
claims: The visible white crystals described in the FAQ are tyrosine, an amino acid.
Tyrosine is released as proteins break down during maturation.
The crystals become larger and more numerous with longer maturation.

lines: Those white crystals in Parmigiano Reggiano are not salt.
The cheese consortium identifies them as tyrosine, an amino acid.
As the cheese matures, enzymes break down milk proteins and release amino acids.
Tyrosine can gather into the little crystals you see inside the cheese.
Longer maturation brings more of them, and larger ones. Even the minimum ageing takes twelve months.
Now look at your next wedge. Do the crystals make it more tempting, or less?

title: A chocolate egg sold for seven thousand pounds

sources.title: Guinness World Records report, 21 March 2012
claims: A 50 kilogram chocolate egg sold for £7,000 at a London charity auction in March 2012.
It was designed by William Curley.
Seven chocolatiers worked for three days.
Fillings included muscovado caramel, Japanese black vinegar, rosemary and olive oil.
The report described a non-jewelled chocolate egg record in 2012, not a current record.

lines: Seven thousand pounds for chocolate. This happened at a London charity auction in twenty twelve.
The egg weighed fifty kilos and was designed by chocolatier William Curley.
Seven chocolatiers spent three days making it.
Inside were fillings including caramel, Japanese black vinegar, rosemary and olive oil.
Guinness reported the non-jewelled chocolate egg record then. This is a historical auction story.
Would you break it open, or keep it untouched? Pick your side.

title: This saffron helped build a skyline

sources.title: Visit Tuscany official tourism: PDO San Gimignano saffron
claims: Saffron trade profits helped some families finance San Gimignano towers.
Trade is documented from the thirteenth century.
The PDO production area is the territory of San Gimignano.
Flower picking, separating stigmas and drying still involve manual work.

lines: A spice helped pay for the towers of an Italian town.
In San Gimignano, saffron trade is documented from the thirteenth century.
Tuscany tourism says some families put their saffron profits into the town's famous towers.
Today, this protected saffron comes from the territory of San Gimignano.
Flowers are picked in the early morning, with delicate work still done by hand.
A skyline with a food story behind it. Would you rather explore the towers, or taste the saffron?
